description: We are a team of enthusiastic first-year BTech students interested in Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, coding, and space technology. We are excited to explore innovative ideas and solve real-world problems using NASA data. We believe in teamwork, creativity, and learning new things. We welcome members who are interested in Python, AI/ML, research, data analysis, and creative problem-solving. Let's learn, innovate, and explore space together!
summary:
AstroGuard is a wrist-worn prototype that tracks an astronaut's heart rate, SpO₂, skin temperature and movement together with cumulative radiation dose. It raises a high-priority alert when the vitals and the dose both point to danger, so crews can act early on Moon and Mars missions.
Project Details (paste in the box)
What it does: An ESP32 reads a MAX30102 (heart rate, SpO₂), a temperature sensor, an MPU6050 (movement) and a radiation sensor. It sends the data to a live dashboard with vitals, a cumulative dose bar and alerts. A buzzer, LED and OLED give local warnings.
Key idea: Alerts are based on combined signals. For example, a rising dose plus abnormal heart rate or temperature triggers a high-priority warning.
Benefits: Earlier detection of health risk and one device for both health and radiation tracking. It also works when communication with Earth is delayed.
Impact: Safer long-duration missions beyond low Earth orbit.
Tools: ESP32, Arduino/C++, [dashboard tech], Bluetooth/Wi-Fi.
Limitations: This is a prototype. A hobby radiation sensor can't match space-grade detectors, so the dose logic was tested with simulated data and NASA open radiation datasets.
details:
AstroGuard: a wearable health and radiation monitor for astronauts

What it does and how it works: AstroGuard is a wrist-worn prototype for astronauts on long space missions. An ESP32 board reads heart rate and SpO₂ (MAX30102), skin temperature (DS18B20 or MLX90614), movement (MPU6050) and radiation counts (Geiger module or PIN-diode sensor). It keeps a running total of radiation dose and sends the data to a live dashboard on a phone or laptop. The wristband also shows readings on an OLED display and warns with a buzzer and LED. A simple rule set, with an optional AI layer, looks for abnormal trends. When a rising dose appears together with an abnormal heart rate or temperature, it raises a high-priority alert.

Benefits: Earlier warning of health risk, one device for both vitals and radiation, and local alerts that work even when communication with Earth is delayed.

Intended impact: Safer Moon, Mars and deep-space missions, where doctors on the ground cannot respond in real time.

Tools, languages and hardware: ESP32, Arduino/C++, [dashboard tools], Bluetooth/Wi-Fi, MAX30102, MPU6050, OLED display, buzzer, battery.

Creativity: It combines health and radiation signals in one wearable and alerts on both signals together, not one sensor at a time.

Factors considered: Low power use, compact size, motion noise on the wrist, limited bandwidth, and the privacy of crew health data.

Limitations: This is a prototype. Hobby radiation sensors cannot match space-grade detectors, so the dose logic was tested with simulated data and NASA open radiation datasets. It is not a certified medical or radiation instrument.
